Hi, everyone. I'm Ryan. I'm here from eDNA Explorer, and I'm going to tell you
about some work we did with community organizations and their work in the LA
River restoration.
So to begin with, the LA River, it's in Los Angeles, California.
It runs from the San Fernando Valley through downtown LA, out to the
river in Long Beach. In the 1930s, there was a really severe flood that
happened, and in order to try to control flooding for the future, they started this
process of channelization along the river.
And today, about 95% of it is now channelized and encased in concrete,
which you can imagine affects the biodiversity in this area.
And so more recently, there's been a push now to remove that concrete and try to
revitalize the LA River.
So this work I'm talking about started in about 2019 with this Protect Our River
organization that brought together a bunch of community groups, land
managers, Indigenous groups along the riverbed, and it was all funded by Metabolic
Studio and CaliDNA at the University of California, Santa Cruz.
And they wanted to go about removing the concrete and seeing how that affected the
biodiversity along the Los Angeles River.
To do this, they turned to eDNA metabarcoding, which is a powerful tool to
monitor and measure biodiversity along here.
Just a brief intro, I'm sure everybody already knows, organisms can shed their DNA
into their surroundings. We can collect it, identify the sequences, and just get
a snapshot, little historical view of what species have been in that area.
For example, like this Muscovy duck
And so where eDNA Explorer comes in-- so for this effort, they
sampled 12 sites along the LA River over seven months and
using six different markers, so really got a snapshot across the tree of life here.
And our platform then is able to take all this data after they've collected it.
We do the sequencing, take care of all the FASTQ controlled
processing, all the taxonomic assignments, all the confidence around those, and
making sure it's as strong as we can, as well as building some community ecology
and machine learning models with this data.
So now I'm going to go over a little overview of what our platform enabled them to
look at,
without having to get into the nitty-gritty of the bioinformatics on their side.
So of course, we can see across the markers they looked at, the various species
that were identified. We incorporate in GBIF data.
They can look at the local area, state level, or national level.
We are working also on having it be able to upload data to GBIF, which we started
recently.
We can also look more specifically at GBIF if you're interested in specific
organisms. For example, there's crawfish, which we identified in several
samples and was corroborated by GBIF in that area.
And as expected, eDNA also was able to identify some that weren't observed in
GBIF, such as this freshwater
jellyfish, which was in about a third of the samples.
This is a really small organism, really hard to see by visual methods.
But with eDNA, we were able to identify it across 12 sites across all sampling
periods, so highlighting the importance of using this in
conjunction with other methods to get more information about the biodiversity.
Can also do some simple longitudinal analysis since they were looking all across
these seven months. Here we can see a variety of organisms identified by the
CO1 marker.
In the summer months and the winter months.
On the top, you can see organisms that were more prevalent in the summer, less
prevalent in the winter, and on the bottom, the inverse, less
prevalent in the summer, more prevalent in the winter.
So again, allowing people to get this overview of their data without having to
know how to manipulate it themselves.
In terms of community modeling, as I mentioned, they were interested in how
concrete affected the biodiversity in
the LA River.
And so we can say that it was quite a strong predictor across
the majority of markers that we looked at.
How we got about this was the platform takes about 400
geospatial data points collected from Google Earth Engine.
This covers things like precipitation, climate, greenness,
human activity, pollutants in the area, as well as a few others,
and the variables that people collect.
So any custom data you want to import will also be included.
We then run a random forest model and help try to model the
beta diversity of this. So you can see here, this is a principal component analysis
of the 18S eukaryotic marker. We see these two communities of channelized
and natural communities as partially channelized, kind of diffusing
across, suggesting that concrete has some impact on the composition
at these areas.
So our platform really enabled these groups, without much of a basis in the actual
science, to really have access to this more advanced tooling and understand their
data.
It's now continually being used to monitor their restoration efforts.
It's also in talks to be used as a baseline pathogen measure for the
upcoming Los Angeles Olympics in 2028.
And also, the various indigenous groups are using it as supporting evidence for
